newsitem.title: USA: Big Three Q2 N. American auto output seen steady.
newsitem.headline: Big Three Q2 N. American auto output seen steady.

text.p: The Big Three U.S. automakers are expected to plan steady production for the second quarter of 1997, but analysts warned Thursday that fierce competition could force them to boost incentives or slash output.

General Motors Corp was the first of Detroit's carmakers to reveal its second quarter North American production estimates Thursday, announcing plans to build 1.55 million cars and trucks -- about flat with a year ago and 7.8 percent above first quarter output.
Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp plan to release their estimates for the April-June period by early next week.

Some analysts said Chrysler may increase its second quarter North American production by 30,000 to 50,000 vehicles above the 752,500 units it built in the second quarter of 1996, due to higher truck output.

"It looks like they're all betting on a strong spring selling season," said Bear Stearns auto analyst Nick Lobaccaro. "Unless the market really hits stride, they're going to have to cut production or add rebates."
The resurgence of Japanese automakers in the U.S. market during the first two months of 1997 has caused analysts to fret about rising dealer inventories of Big Three passenger cars.

Chrysler, escalating the price war in passenger cars, this week began offering its dealers up to $600 in incentives for each car sold this month. The incentives allow dealers to negotiate better deals for buyers.
Salomon Brothers analyst Jack Kirnan said Thursday in a conference call that he expects incentive activity to increase.

"In fact we'll probably see some other marketing actions announced by the car companies shortly and or we'll see somep production cuts announced for the second and third quarters," Kirnan said. "That's the stuff that good stock performance is not made of."

In the past week, Chrysler shares have fallen 8.6 percent, closing up 62.5 cents on Thursday at $31.75 on the New York Stock Exchange. Ford shares were off 6.7 percent for the week, closing off 25 cents Thursday at 33.375, while GM shares closed off $1.25 Thursday at $56, down 4.7 percent for the week.

GM and Ford said Thursday they had no immediate plans to match Chrysler's dealer incentives. A GM spokesman said the automaker is in the midst of launching several new models that will not need incentives.
"We'll see what kind of impact this has," Ford spokeswoman Joy Wolfe said of the Chrysler dealer incentive plan. "It's not something that requires any immediate change in what we're doing."

Analysts said Ford, which has experienced a 7.7 percent decline in passenger car sales so far this year, was the most likely to cut car production. GM car sales were off 4.7 percent, while Chrysler passenger car sales were off 1.1 percent.

But Burnham Securities analyst David Healy said he believes the Big Three at this point are more willing to spend on increased incentives than to cut production because overall sales remain strong, running at a 15.3 million unit rate in February.

For all U.S. automakers, including Japanese transplant makers, McDonald & Co analyst Gregory Kagay said he expects an overall second quarter production increase of one to two perent over the year-ago period.
